title: Review: Potential dividers; Progressive waves; Intensity; Electromagnetic spectrum
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: W12-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; W01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; W01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; W12-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL07-1#N.5, W01-1#N.1, W01-uk1#N.10, W02-1#N.2, W12-1#N.13, EL07-1#N.3, W01-1#N.15, W01-uk1#N.3, W02-1#N.14, W12-1#N.2, EL07-1#N.8, W01-uk1#N.5. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Point source
items.clue: Small emitter treated as sending its power out equally in all directions.

items.label: Wavelength
items.clue: Distance between the nearest points that move in step, such as crest to crest.

items.label: Transverse wave
items.clue: Has oscillations perpendicular to the direction in which energy travels, as on a string.

items.label: Intensity
items.clue: Power arriving per unit area on a surface perpendicular to the wave's direction, in W m⁻².

questions.stem: A potentiometer has a uniform resistance track connected across a 9.0 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected between one end of the track and the sliding contact, which is one third of the way along the track from that end. What does the voltmeter read?
A loudspeaker plays a steady note to a listener 5 m away in a room with still air. Which of the following travels from the loudspeaker to the listener?

options.text: Energy, passed along by air molecules that vibrate about fixed positions
Air molecules, pushed across the room from the loudspeaker to the ear
Sound particles, which the loudspeaker gives off and the air carries
An electromagnetic signal, which needs no air to carry it across

questions.stem: A loudspeaker emits a steady 500 Hz note. Two microphones are placed on a straight line from the loudspeaker, 0.17 m apart. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. How do the oscillations detected by the two microphones compare?

options.text: They are in antiphase, π rad apart.
They are a quarter of a cycle, π/2 rad, apart.
They are in phase, as the note has one frequency.
They are an eighth of a cycle, π/4 rad, apart.

questions.stem: Predict first. Which statement describes the nature of electromagnetic waves?

options.text: Oscillations of the particles of the medium they travel through, so they cannot cross a vacuum
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel faster in a vacuum the higher their frequency
Streams of tiny charged particles given out by the source, which can travel through a vacuum
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel

questions.stem: A small source sends out sound equally in all directions. At 2.0 m from the source the intensity is 6.0 × 10⁻³ W m⁻². Ignoring reflections and absorption, what is the intensity 3.0 m from the source?

An LDR and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. In the room's light the LDR's resistance is 900 Ω. What does an ideal voltmeter across the 300 Ω resistor read?
questions.explanation: The pd divides in proportion to resistance: 6.0 × 300/(300 + 900) = 1.5 V.

questions.stem: A vibrator sends waves along a stretched string at constant tension. At 25 Hz the wavelength is 0.80 m. The frequency is raised to 100 Hz. What is the new wavelength, and how long does a wave now take to travel 4.0 m along the string?
questions.explanation: v = fλ = 25 × 0.80 = 20 m s⁻¹, unchanged. New λ = 20/100 = 0.20 m; time = 4.0/20 = 0.20 s, the same as before.

questions.stem: Two points on a progressive wave of wavelength 1.2 m are 0.40 m apart along the direction of travel. What is the phase difference between their oscillations?
questions.explanation: Right. Δx/λ = 0.40/1.2 = ⅓ cycle, and ⅓ × 2π = 2π/3 rad (120°).

questions.stem: In a vacuum, the microwaves in a speed camera have a wavelength of 3.0 cm, and the light from a yellow lamp has a wavelength of 600 nm. How do their frequencies compare?

options.text: The microwave frequency is 5 × 10⁴ times the light frequency, since f rises with λ.
They are equal, because both waves travel at the same speed, c, in a vacuum.
The light frequency is 5 × 10⁴ times the microwave frequency, since f = c/λ.
The light frequency is higher, because light travels faster than microwaves.

questions.explanation: Same c for both, so f ∝ 1/λ. Ratio = (3.0 × 10⁻² m)/(600 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 5 × 10⁴: the light's frequency is that many times higher.

questions.stem: Sunlight of intensity 1.0 × 10³ W m⁻² falls perpendicularly on a flat solar cell of area 150 cm². At what rate does the sunlight deliver energy to the cell?

An LDR and a 10 kΩ fixed resistor are in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected across the fixed resistor. The LDR's resistance is 50 kΩ in the dark and 1.0 kΩ in bright light. What does the voltmeter read in each case?

options.text: 5.0 V in the dark; 0.55 V in bright light
5.5 V in the dark; 1.0 V in bright light
1.0 V in the dark; 5.5 V in bright light

questions.explanation: Dark: 6.0 × 10/(10 + 50) = 1.0 V. Bright: 6.0 × 10/(10 + 1.0) = 5.5 V. The fixed resistor's share rises as the LDR's resistance falls.

questions.stem: Two displacement–time graphs, P and Q, show the oscillations of two points on a wave. Both have a period of 6.0 ms. Each crest of Q comes 1.0 ms after the matching crest of P. What is the phase difference between P and Q?
